question: Is a convert sinful for hiding his Islam, and how should he practice where he can't reveal it?
asked: I am from a village in India and I accepted Islam three years ago, and I have been listening to your lectures for the last five years. In my town there is not a single Muslim or a masjid. My parents, friends and family do not know about my conversion. How do I practice the deen, because I don't know much about the deen and I don't have access to people who can teach me? As well, I cannot reveal my Islam right now, so am I sinful for hiding my Islam, since the situation here is not very good?
answer:
This question really touched me immensely. To me it was a very emotional question; subhanAllah, it really made me pause.

First and foremost, we thank Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala for the freedoms that we have to pray and fast and be Muslim, alhamdulillah. We thank Allah that we are not in such a position that our very Islam is a difficulty to reveal.

And secondly, we thank Allah for the blessings of the internet, which has allowed the da'wah to be spread across this globe to people that we have no contact with. This is a brother who for five years has been researching and listening to lectures, and Allah guided him to Islam, even though he has never met a Muslim in his small village. He has access to the internet, he's listening to these lectures, and he got the email from these lectures to give us. SubhanAllah, what a world we live in! This is Allah's blessing, that communication has opened the world now, and the whole world literally is a village. Even the village is on the superhighway that is connected.

Now, as to the response to the question, I say to this brother: first and foremost, obviously, we thank Allah, and you should thank Allah, for having guided you to Islam in such difficult circumstances. And realize, my dear brother in Islam, that all of us love you for the sake of Allah; even if you have not met us, we love you.

Realize that your situation is atypical, and **you are obliged to do only what you are capable of doing, without bringing any undue harm or severe repercussions upon yourself, or your movements, or your freedom.** It's not just a matter of life and death, or else you have to do it. No, the Shari'ah allows you, in case of harm that is unnecessarily burdensome on you, that is not something that you can bear reasonably. Who gets to define what is reasonable? Only you, because you have to answer to Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala for what you have done.

If a difficulty is too unreasonable for you to bear... not just a matter of life and death. Obviously life and death is clear-cut: the haram becomes halal, even if somebody forces you to commit shirk, as Allah says in the Qur'an:

> إِلَّا مَنْ أُكْرِهَ وَقَلْبُهُ مُطْمَئِنٌّ بِالْإِيمَانِ

That's a clear-cut scenario. But the Shari'ah allows concessions even of a lesser nature. If you choose to do so, it is up to you. You don't have to, but the Shari'ah allows you to do so.

And I wanted to quote you in some detail, but it is all from Ibn Taymiyyah, the famous scholar. He has a book, Minhaj al-Sunnah, volume 5, 110, for those that are interested. It is a very long passage; I have summarized it. He said that Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala has informed us in the Qur'an on multiple occasions that He does not place a burden on a soul more than what the soul can bear:

> لَا نُكَلِّفُ نَفْسًا إِلَّا وُسْعَهَا
> لَا يُكَلِّفُ اللَّهُ نَفْسًا إِلَّا مَا آتَاهَا
> فَاتَّقُوا اللَّهَ مَا اسْتَطَعْتُمْ
> رَبَّنَا وَلَا تُحَمِّلْنَا مَا لَا طَاقَةَ لَنَا بِهِ

All of these verses he mentions. And then he says: and therefore the kuffar who have heard of the message of the Prophet ﷺ, living in the lands of kuffar, and they know that the Prophet ﷺ is true, and believe in him, and believe in what has come to him, they should fear Allah as much as they can, like Najashi and others.

Najashi was the emperor of Abyssinia, and he converted to Islam. Ibn Taymiyyah says: Najashi was not able to perform the hijrah. Najashi could not practice Islam openly. Najashi did not have anyone to teach him all of the Shari'ah of Islam. And yet he is a mu'min, from the people of Jannah.

So too he mentions the famous person in the Qur'an: there was a mu'min in the family of Fir'awn who hid his iman. This person that hid his iman is considered to be of the people of Jannah. And likewise the wife of Fir'awn, Asiya. And likewise Yusuf 'alayhis salam, when he was put as the minister over the people of Egypt: all of them were kuffar, and he could not deal with them fully according to the teachings of Islam, even though he called them to Islam.

Then he goes back to Najashi. As for Najashi, he was the king of the Christians, and he realized his people would not accept Islam. And therefore, when he died, no one prayed janazah for him. Not a single person prayed janazah for Najashi in his hometown. So our Prophet ﷺ led the Muslims outside and said to the believers, "Your brother, a righteous man, Najashi, has died. We will pray janazah over him," in Medina. This is janazah 'ala al-gha'ib.

And Najashi did not make hijrah, did not do jihad, did not perform Hajj. In fact, it was not even narrated that he prayed the five prayers, or fasted the month of Ramadan, or gave zakah. This is Ibn Taymiyyah writing, by the way. Najashi: it is not narrated that he prayed, or gave zakah, or fasted Ramadan. And we know for certain that he could not judge in accordance with the Shari'ah of Allah over his people, because his people would not have let him do that; his people would have stopped him.

> وَلَا نُكَلِّفُ نَفْسًا إِلَّا وُسْعَهَا

So he goes on and on, and he therefore says that Najashi was excused because of the pressures on him, and he is a believer, despite the fact that he did not do what other believers did. Even in Abyssinia, by the way, his circumstances were different.

And this leads us to the issue now: well then, when are you obliged to migrate? When must you leave your land? Our scholars mention two conditions necessary, and this is based on the verse in the Qur'an. Allah says: when the angels come to take the souls of those who used to commit sins, the angels will say, "What were you doing?" And the people will say, "It's not our fault. We were persecuted in the land; we were weak in the land." The angels will say, "Wasn't the land of Allah vast? You could migrate somewhere else." Then Allah says: they cannot find a way out, men, women and children who genuinely are trapped. Allah says these people, I shall forgive them. 'Asa here means "I shall forgive them":

> فَأُولَٰئِكَ عَسَى اللَّهُ أَن يَعْفُوَ عَنْهُمْ

Therefore, dear brother in Islam, watching from your village in India, two conditions:

1. Number one: if you are not able to practice Islam at a bare minimal level, which means say the prayers, give zakah, fast Ramadan, you're not forced to commit major sin. Such as in this country of America, we have the freedom. If you have that freedom, it is not wajib to migrate. If you don't have that freedom, condition one is met. Check.
2. Condition two: do you have the capability to leave that land? Are you physically and emotionally and financially capable? Are you able to leave, or do you have nowhere to go, you don't have the finances? If you are able to leave...

So if both conditions are met, then hijrah is obligatory. If either condition is not met, hijrah is not obligatory; you don't have to migrate.

So, dear brother in Islam, if you are not allowed to pray, and you're not allowed to fast, and you cannot declare your Islam, but you are not able to migrate, which appears to be the situation, your circumstances (you don't have any place to go, you are in a small village, you don't have the finances to go anywhere), in this case you must worship Allah to the best of your ability: fattaqu Allaha ma istata'tum. And only you know how far you can go.

If your life is in danger, you are not obliged to put your life in danger. If your life is under physical threat and harm, if they will beat you, you don't have to do anything that will cause that beating. **It is not an obligation to announce your Islam publicly; it is not a condition.** You say the shahada privately. You can whisper the shahada when you're all alone: La ilaha illallah, Muhammadur Rasulullah.

You can try to pray to the best of your ability, with your door locked, when you're alone. Try to pray when nobody is watching, or find a place where nobody is watching. And learn how to pray from YouTube videos. You say you're watching my lectures and other lectures online; there are plenty of lectures on how to pray. Learn how to pray. If you're able to fast Ramadan without giving yourself away, do so. And if you're able to do other things... as for giving zakah, inshallah, that is possible for you to do. My point is: do whatever you can in your circumstance.

My dear brother, as well: if you're able to go to a neighboring village where there are Muslims and a masjid, and your identity can remain unknown from the first village, find a Muslim community, because finding brothers really helps out. Perhaps one of them will be able to help you get away from this situation and open up other opportunities for you.

But the point is that you must try your best within your means, and Allah will not punish you for what is beyond your means. So you believe in your heart, alhamdulillah, this is the main thing, but you must follow up that belief with whatever actions you are capable of doing. And whatever you're not capable of, then Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala will forgive you. And make du'a for your situation; we will make du'a for you.

And we want you to know that you are our brother in Islam, even if you're watching 5,000 miles away, and we may never meet in this world. Inshallah ta'ala, we will meet in the akhirah. You are doing a type of jihad that is inconceivable for us. You are doing a type of jihad, living amongst people that might potentially kill you. We know what is happening in that land now. Living amongst people where you're scared your own family and friends might turn against you any day, and only you know the pressure you are in. And for you to find Islam in the midst of this environment, subhanAllah, Allah has willed good for you, that you have found Islam in such an environment. So thank Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala.

And I hope that that example serves as a role model for all of us here. Here is a person who wants to pray. He's asking, "How can I pray? I'm all alone." What excuse do we have? He wants to practice Islam in a place where he might be killed for practicing Islam. What excuse do we have? So I pray that Allah blesses you, and I pray that Allah blesses all of us.
